title: Stepwise Toolflow & SDK Interaction Playbook (hosted API sketch)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for exploring a stepwise toolflow pattern for the Hosted API: an incremental, resumable streaming surface that makes tool calls explicit, supports partial structured outputs, and gives client SDKs small, composable hooks for UX-critical behavior (progress, errors, retries).

Context / motivation:
- We have many streaming/SDK PRDs focused on progressive output but they often assume a single continuous text stream or opaque partial frames.
- Product asks: make tool calls first-class without forcing synchronous blocking; let clients show intermediate structured actions and let servers roll forward or backfill results as they become available.
- Engineering asks: minimal protocol surface, backwards compatible with current streaming wire format, low overhead to implement in runtime.

High-level idea (one-sentence):
Emit a sequence of discrete "steps" (frames) during a streaming response. Steps are typed (text, action-intent, tool-call, tool-result, checkpoint, end) with lightweight monotonic IDs so clients can render partial UIs, request resume or reconciliation, and map telemetry to user-visible transitions.

Design goals (ranked):
1) Ergonomic client SDKs: tiny JS/Go/py helpers that hide reconnection and replay complexity.
2) Deterministic reconciliation: when resuming after a disconnect, clients can dedupe and merge frames without losing tool results.
3) Explicit tool semantics: tool calls are explicit frames that can be executed by client or proxied by Redwood (policy-driven).
4) Low-latency first: payload format should not increase RTT for initial tokens.
5) Observability hooks: every frame carries a trace id, model-version, kernel-profile tag.

Step types (sketch):
- meta: initial handshake; contains request_id, prompt hash, model/version, estimated token budget.
- text: plain incremental text with offsets (start,end) for partial edits; used for free text and natural language generation.
- action-intent: small structured JSON describing an intended action (e.g., {"type":"CREATE_CALENDAR","summary":"Lunch"}). No side effects yet.
- tool-call: declarative call frame describing function signature and arguments. Includes call_id and execution_policy (client|server|ask).
- tool-result: result frame referencing call_id with success|error and payload (structured).
- checkpoint: durable snapshot of conversation state (lightweight KV or pointer to persisted snapshot id). Useful for long-running sessions.
- end: terminal frame with aggregate status.

Wire considerations:
- Keep frames as newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) for streaming compatibility. First byte is meta.
- Each frame must have: frame_id (monotonic string), prev_frame_id (optional), timestamp, trace_id, model_tag. This adds ~150B/frame overhead at most.
- For clients that want minimal overhead, server can fall back to current token stream where text frames are emitted as usual and action/tool frames are embedded as special markers.

SDK ergonomics (JS prototyping notes):
- Primary primitive: onFrame(cb) rather than onToken; SDK exposes high-level events: onTextDelta, onActionIntent, onToolCall, onToolResult, onCheckpoint, onEnd.
- Small helper: reconcileFrames(localState, frames[]) -> deterministic merged output. Clients get an idempotent apply function.
- Reconnect strategy: resume from last-acknowledged frame_id. Server will re-emit from next frame or fast-forward with a checkpoint frame.

Example JS surface (informal):
const stream = client.createStream({ prompt })
stream.on('actionIntent', (intent) => renderIntent(intent))
stream.on('toolCall', async (call) => {
  if (call.execution_policy === 'client') {
    // SDK helper executes and returns result back to server via /respond-tool-result
    const res = await localExec(call.signature, call.args)
    await client.respondToolResult(call.call_id, res)
  }
})
// reconnect
stream.on('disconnect', async (lastFrameId) => {
  const resumed = await client.resumeStream(sessionId, lastFrameId)
  resumed.on('frame', applyFrame)
})

Tool call policy exploration:
- client: call executed by local client (good for access to user tokens, devices). Server emits tool-call then expects tool-result submitted.
- server-proxy: Redwood can act as executor if customer opts in (useful for managed connectors). Must include allowlist and audit logs.
- ask: server will pause generation and surface a UI prompt to user (or SDK) for explicit approval; useful for high-risk actions.

Structured output model:
- Use a common typed envelope: {"type":"tool-result","call_id":"abc","schema":"application/vnd.redwood.v1+json","payload":{...}}
- Encourage model output to reference schemas by short names; SDKs ship validators for common schemas (calendar, http-call, file-create).
- For large results, tool-result can include a blob pointer: {"payload_ref":"s3://..."} and small summary in payload.

Backpressure and UX:
- Provide client hint headers: X-Client-Latency-Budget, X-Target-Render-Fidelity. Server uses these to choose batch/emit behavior.
- SDK exposes 'softProgress' events to enable UX placeholders while waiting for tool-results.

Resumability and idempotence:
- Frames are monotonic and durable for the lifetime of session_id + ttl. Clients resume by sending last_received_frame_id. Server can: (a) re-emit missing frames, (b) emit a checkpoint frame with consolidated state if original frames are evicted.
- For tool-calls, call_id must be globally unique within session. If client retries a tool-call submission, server will dedupe by call_id.

Observability and telemetry mapping:
- Each frame includes debug_tags: model_hash, kernel_profile, sequence_position. These are surfaced in Console timelines.
- Telemetry events to record: tool-call-latency, tool-executor (client|server), tool-error-class, resume_count, reconnect_cause.

Migration strategy from current streaming approach:
1) Start with opt-in experiment: server emits action-intent frames only (no tool-call) for a small set of models. SDKs parse action-intent and render UI.
2) Add tool-call frames but default execution_policy to 'ask' to avoid accidental effects.
3) Offer server-exec for partner customers with audit logging.

Open questions / risks (notes to self):
- Security: how to ensure server-proxied tool execution does not leak customer data? Need per-connector allowlists + KMS audit.
- Backward compatibility: how many clients will ignore new frames and treat stream as text? Plan for graceful degradation.
- Cost: more frames => higher telemetry/ingest cost. Need efficient encoding (short keys).
- UX complexity: many clients will struggle to show mid-stream actions - need SDK default renderers.

Next steps / action items (very rough):
- Engineering: prototype NDJSON frames in runtime (HOSTED-1023) - Jordan owns spike (2w).
- SDK: ship small JS helper library implementing resume/reconcile primitives (Kai owns).
- Product: define 3 example schemas (calendar.create, http.call, file.save) and validation rules (Marisol).
- Security: doc connector policy for server-exec (security review required).

References / links (working):
- Slack thread: #hosted-api-streaming (see messages around Nov 2025)
- GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/hosted-api/pull/789
- Related ticket: HOSTED-1023

Notes to self: this is intentionally pragmatic: keep frame vocabulary small, make SDKs do heavy lifting, avoid forcing new semantics on existing users. The aim is to incrementally enable powerful tool-driven UIs without large runtime complexity.

-- Aisha
